intro.title: Forty-six years on the brink
body: In 1945 the United States and the Soviet Union stood together over a defeated Germany. Within three years they were rivals, each armed with a different idea of how the world should be run, and soon each armed with the atomic bomb.

Their armies never fought each other directly. Instead the Cold War was fought by threat and bluff in Europe, and by real wars in Korea, Vietnam, Afghanistan, Angola and many other places. Millions died in these proxy wars, most of them civilians.
It ended almost without a shot. In 1989 the peoples of Eastern Europe pulled down their communist governments, the Berlin Wall fell, and in December 1991 the Soviet Union itself was dissolved.
tips: Press play to watch the world split into blocs and come back together. The map flies to each crisis.

Dark blue is NATO, light blue other US allies. Dark red is the Soviet Union, red its satellites in the Warsaw Pact, orange the other communist states. Gold is non-aligned, grey neutral, green the countries whose communist rule ended in 1989–91.
Zoom into Berlin to see the four sectors and the Wall. Two animated scenes: the Berlin Airlift and the fall of South Vietnam in 1975.

eras.title: From allies to rivals
eras.text: The victors of 1945 fall out over Germany and Eastern Europe. An Iron Curtain descends, and Berlin is blockaded.

eras.title: The war turns hot in Asia
eras.text: The Soviet bomb, a communist China and a war in Korea. In Indochina the French are driven out.

eras.title: Brinkmanship
eras.text: Hungary is crushed, Sputnik flies, a Wall divides Berlin. In October 1962 the world comes closest to nuclear war.

eras.title: Vietnam and détente
eras.text: The United States fights and loses a long war in Vietnam. Moscow and Washington begin to talk and limit their weapons.

eras.title: Proxy wars and a second freeze
eras.text: The rivalry spreads to Africa, Central America and Afghanistan. By 1983 fear of nuclear war is back.

eras.title: Gorbachev and the end
eras.text: Reform in Moscow, revolutions across Eastern Europe in 1989, and the end of the Soviet Union in 1991.

ask.persona: a careful, even-handed historian of the Cold War who explains it to a curious listener. You give the Soviet, American and Third World sides their due, treat the dead of the proxy wars with seriousness, and say when numbers are estimates
